text: When did GDPR come into force?

options.text: January 1, 2012
March 15, 2016

explanation: GDPR came into force on May 25, 2018, replacing the 1995 EU Data Protection Directive. Organizations had a two-year transition period from when it was adopted in April 2016.

text: A US-based company sells products to customers in Germany. Does GDPR apply to the processing of those German customers' data?

options.text: No, because the company is based in the US
Only if the company has offices in Europe
Yes, GDPR applies based on where the data subjects are located, not where the organization is based
Only if the company has more than 250 employees

explanation: GDPR has broad territorial scope. It applies to any organization processing personal data of individuals in the EU/EEA, regardless of the organization's location. Processing data of EU residents triggers GDPR compliance obligations.

text: A company violates GDPR by processing data without any lawful basis. What is the maximum fine they could face?

options.text: €2 million
€10 million or 2% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher
€20 million or 4% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher
€50,000 fixed fine

explanation: Processing without a lawful basis is a violation of Article 6, one of GDPR's fundamental requirements. This falls under the upper tier of fines: up to €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher.

text: Which GDPR principle requires organizations to be able to demonstrate compliance with all other GDPR principles?

options.text: Data Minimisation
Purpose Limitation
Accountability
Storage Limitation

explanation: The Accountability principle (Article 5(2)) is the meta-principle of GDPR — it requires organizations not just to comply, but to be able to demonstrate compliance. This drives the requirement for documentation, DPIAs, Records of Processing Activities, and training records.

text: Which of the following is personal data under GDPR?

options.text: A report showing that 10,000 users visited a website last month (no identifiers)
The name of a business
An IP address that can be linked to an individual
Truly anonymized salary statistics

explanation: An IP address that can be linked to an identifiable individual is personal data under GDPR. The CJEU confirmed this in the Breyer case. Aggregate statistics with no re-identification possibility and business names (without individual identifiers) are generally not personal data.

text: Your organization replaces customer names with unique ID numbers in a database for analysis. Is this data still subject to GDPR?

options.text: No, once names are removed the data is anonymous
Yes, pseudonymized data is still personal data because it can be re-identified using the key
Only if the analysis identifies patterns about specific individuals
No, GDPR only applies to data that directly identifies people

explanation: Pseudonymization replaces identifying information with a code but the data can be re-linked using the key. GDPR explicitly addresses pseudonymization (Recital 26) and confirms it remains personal data. Only truly irreversible anonymization removes data from GDPR's scope.

text: Which of the following is NOT a special category of personal data under GDPR?

options.text: An employee's sickness absence records
A customer's political donation history
A customer's home address
An employee's trade union membership

explanation: A home address is personal data but not special category data. Special categories include health data (sickness records), political opinions (donation history), and trade union membership. These categories receive heightened protection due to their sensitivity.

text: An organization implements a fingerprint-based door access system for employees. Under GDPR, fingerprint data used to uniquely identify employees is classified as:

options.text: Regular personal data requiring only a standard lawful basis
Special category data (biometric data) requiring both a lawful basis and a special category condition
Non-personal data since it belongs to the organization's security system
Sensitive data but not special category data

explanation: Biometric data processed to uniquely identify a natural person is explicitly listed as special category data in GDPR Article 9. Processing requires both a lawful basis under Article 6 AND a specific condition under Article 9, making this a significant compliance consideration for biometric access systems.

text: How many lawful bases does GDPR provide for processing personal data?
explanation: GDPR Article 6 provides six lawful bases: (1) Consent, (2) Contract, (3) Legal Obligation, (4) Vital Interests, (5) Public Task, and (6) Legitimate Interests. One of these must apply to every instance of personal data processing.

text: A company processes employee health insurance enrollment data to comply with a mandatory employment benefits law. Which lawful basis is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Consent
Contract
Legal Obligation
Legitimate Interests

explanation: Legal Obligation (Article 6(1)(c)) is the correct basis when processing is required to comply with a law. Relying on consent in an employment context is problematic due to the power imbalance. Legal Obligation is more appropriate and more stable (it cannot be withdrawn like consent).

text: A company relies on Legitimate Interests as the lawful basis for email marketing to existing customers. Before doing so, they must complete what?

options.text: Nothing — legitimate interests always applies to existing customer relationships
A three-part Legitimate Interests Assessment (LIA) balancing the company's interests against the individuals' rights
A Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA)
Registration with the national supervisory authority

explanation: Legitimate Interests requires a documented three-part test: (1) Is there a legitimate interest? (2) Is processing necessary for it? (3) Do the individual's interests and rights override the legitimate interest? This 'balancing test' must be documented before relying on this basis.

text: Which of the following represents VALID consent under GDPR?

options.text: A pre-ticked checkbox on a registration form
A clause buried in Terms & Conditions that users must accept to use a service
An unticked checkbox with a clear, specific statement about what data will be used for
Continued use of a website after a notification that data is being collected

explanation: Valid GDPR consent requires a clear affirmative action (not pre-ticked), specific purpose, informed understanding, and unambiguous indication of agreement. Options A, B, and D all fail the requirements for valid consent.

text: An individual withdraws their consent for marketing communications. What must the organization do?

options.text: Process the withdrawal request within 30 days
Stop processing their data for marketing purposes immediately
Send a confirmation email and stop processing within 28 days
Anonymize the data within 30 days

explanation: Under GDPR, when consent is withdrawn, processing must cease immediately for the purpose covered by that consent. Withdrawal must be as easy as giving consent. Organizations cannot impose delays — they must stop immediately.

text: An employer asks all employees to sign a consent form agreeing to monitoring of their work emails. Why might this consent be problematic under GDPR?

options.text: Employees cannot consent to email monitoring under any circumstances
Consent in an employment context may not be freely given due to the power imbalance between employer and employee
Email monitoring requires a different form of consent than a standard form
Only the Data Protection Officer can collect consent in employment contexts

explanation: GDPR Recital 43 notes that consent should not be a valid lawful basis where there is a clear imbalance between the data subject and controller, especially where the controller is a public authority. Employment relationships typically have this imbalance — employees may not feel free to refuse without fear of consequences. Legal Obligation or Legitimate Interests would be more appropriate bases.

text: The data minimisation principle requires that personal data collected must be:

options.text: Comprehensive, covering all possible future uses
Adequate, relevant, and limited to what is necessary for the purpose
Encrypted and backed up
Shared with supervisory authorities upon request

explanation: Data minimisation (Article 5(1)(c)) requires that personal data be adequate (sufficient for the purpose), relevant (pertaining to the purpose), and limited to what is necessary. Organizations should not collect more data than they need, even if more data might be useful.

text: A company collects customer email addresses to send order confirmations. Can they use these addresses to send promotional newsletters?

options.text: Yes, because the customer provided their email address to the company
No — using order confirmation emails for marketing is a different, incompatible purpose without separate consent or lawful basis
Yes, if the newsletters are related to similar products
Only if the newsletter contains an unsubscribe link

explanation: Purpose limitation prevents repurposing data for different, incompatible uses. Collecting email for transactional communications (order confirmations) does not authorize using it for marketing. A separate lawful basis (typically consent or legitimate interests with a right to opt out) is needed for marketing.

text: Which GDPR principle addresses how long personal data should be retained?

options.text: Data Minimisation
Integrity and Confidentiality
Storage Limitation
Purpose Limitation

explanation: Storage Limitation (Article 5(1)(e)) requires that personal data be kept no longer than necessary for the purposes for which it was processed. Organizations must have documented retention schedules and actively delete or anonymize data when the retention period expires.

text: An organization's marketing team wants to keep a mailing list of contacts 'just in case' they run a campaign in the future, even though the last meaningful contact was 3 years ago. Is this compliant with GDPR?

options.text: Yes, as long as the data is stored securely
Yes, if consent was originally obtained for marketing
No — 'just in case' is not a specific purpose; data cannot be retained indefinitely without a current, legitimate reason
Yes, because marketing campaigns are a legitimate business interest

explanation: GDPR's storage limitation principle prohibits retaining data indefinitely 'just in case.' There must be a current, documented purpose for retention. Where consent has lapsed (no recent interaction) or was never updated, retaining the data without a lawful basis is a GDPR violation.

text: Within how many days must an organization respond to a Subject Access Request (SAR)?

options.text: 14 days
30 days (with possible extension for complex requests)
60 days
72 hours

explanation: Organizations must respond to Subject Access Requests within one calendar month (approximately 30 days). For complex or multiple requests, this can be extended by two additional months with written notice to the individual explaining the reason.

text: A data subject requests erasure of their data. Under which circumstance can the organization REFUSE this request?

options.text: The data is stored in a backup system that is hard to update
Deleting the data would take significant resources
The data is needed to comply with a legal obligation or for the establishment of legal claims
The data subject has not provided a specific reason for the request

explanation: The Right to Erasure is not absolute. Organizations can refuse if they need the data to comply with a legal obligation, to establish, exercise, or defend legal claims, or for other specific grounds in Article 17(3). Technical difficulty or resource cost are not valid grounds for refusal.

text: A customer objects to their personal data being used for direct marketing. What is the organization's correct response?

options.text: Assess the objection and respond within 30 days
Continue processing if they have a compelling legitimate interest
Stop processing for direct marketing immediately — the right to object to direct marketing is absolute
Ask the customer to provide evidence supporting their objection

explanation: Under GDPR Article 21(3), when an individual objects to direct marketing processing, the organization MUST stop processing for that purpose. Unlike objections to processing based on legitimate interests (where the controller can override if compelling grounds exist), the right to object to direct marketing is unconditional and absolute.

text: What does 'Privacy by Default' require under GDPR Article 25?

options.text: All privacy settings should default to sharing the maximum amount of data
By default, only the minimum personal data necessary should be processed — individuals should not have to opt out of protection
Organizations should default to not collecting any personal data
Data subjects should default to having all rights waived unless they opt in

explanation: Privacy by Default means systems and processes should, by default, process only the minimum personal data necessary. Users should not have to take extra steps to protect their privacy — the protective settings should be the default, with users opting IN to share more data rather than having to opt out.

text: When must a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) be conducted?

options.text: Only after a data breach has occurred
Annually for all data processing activities
Before commencing processing that is likely to result in high risk to individuals' rights and freedoms
Only for processing of special category data

explanation: A DPIA (Article 35) is mandatory before beginning processing that is 'likely to result in a high risk' to individuals. This includes systematic profiling, large-scale special category data processing, and systematic monitoring. It must be conducted BEFORE the processing begins — this is a core aspect of Privacy by Design.

text: Personal data can be transferred freely to a country outside the EU/EEA if that country has received what from the European Commission?

options.text: A favorable trade agreement
An Adequacy Decision
Standard Contractual Clauses
A Binding Corporate Rules approval

explanation: An Adequacy Decision (Article 45) is the simplest transfer mechanism — the European Commission has assessed that a third country provides an equivalent level of data protection to GDPR. Data can flow as freely as within the EU. Examples include the UK, Canada (commercial), Japan, and South Korea.

text: Your company's US-based parent corporation needs access to the EU subsidiary's employee database for HR management. No adequacy decision exists for general US transfers. What mechanism should be used?

options.text: No mechanism needed — intra-company transfers are exempt from GDPR
Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) or Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs)
Verbal agreement between legal teams
Anonymize all data before transfer

explanation: Intra-company transfers across borders are still subject to GDPR restrictions. For transfers to the US (where no blanket adequacy exists), organizations must use approved transfer mechanisms. SCCs are the most common choice; BCRs are appropriate for multinational corporate groups but require regulatory approval.

text: Under GDPR, within how many hours of becoming aware of a personal data breach must an organization notify its supervisory authority (where the breach poses a risk to individuals)?

options.text: 24 hours
48 hours
72 hours
7 days

explanation: GDPR Article 33 requires notification to the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of a breach (where the breach poses a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms). Crucially, these are calendar hours — not business hours — so weekends and holidays count.

text: Which of the following incidents qualifies as a personal data breach under GDPR?

options.text: An employee accidentally deletes a spreadsheet containing customer contact details, and no backup exists
A vendor proposes a new pricing model for data storage
A power outage causes a 2-hour system downtime with no data loss
A customer updates their email address in your system

explanation: Accidental deletion of personal data without backup is a breach of availability and integrity — meeting GDPR's definition of a personal data breach. A power outage with no data loss is not a breach. Pricing proposals and data updates are not breaches.

text: An encrypted laptop is stolen. The encryption key was not compromised. Is supervisory authority notification likely required?

options.text: Yes, all theft of devices requires immediate notification
No — if the data is properly encrypted and the key is secure, the breach is unlikely to pose a risk to individuals and notification may not be required
Yes, but only if the laptop contains special category data
No notification is ever required for device theft

explanation: GDPR's breach notification threshold depends on whether the breach poses a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms. Properly encrypted data cannot be accessed by an unauthorized person, meaning the breach is unlikely to pose such a risk. Notification may not be required — but the breach must still be documented internally.

text: You receive an email from a customer demanding that you 'immediately delete all information you have about me.' What is the correct action?

options.text: Delete all their records immediately to avoid non-compliance
Ignore the request if you believe they have agreed to your terms of service
Route the request immediately to the privacy team/DPO — do not action it yourself without authorization
Reply explaining your data retention policy and take no further action

explanation: This is a Right to Erasure (Right to be Forgotten) request under GDPR Article 17. It must be formally processed by the privacy team, who will assess whether grounds for erasure exist and provide a proper written response. Employees should never act on rights requests unilaterally — they require coordinated processing.

text: Under GDPR Article 30, which organizations are required to maintain Records of Processing Activities (RoPA)?

options.text: Only organizations with more than 5,000 employees
Only organizations that process special category data
All organizations, with limited exceptions for small organizations processing non-risky data
Only public sector organizations

explanation: Article 30 requires all controllers and processors to maintain Records of Processing Activities. There is a limited exception for organizations with fewer than 250 employees, BUT this exception does not apply if the processing carries risks to data subjects' rights, involves special category data, or is not occasional. In practice, most organizations — including small ones — must maintain a RoPA.
